newsitem.title: USA: Du Pont mental state focus of sentence hearing.
newsitem.headline: Du Pont mental state focus of sentence hearing.

text.p: Millionaire John du Pont's mental condition is improving but he should still be treated in a psychiatric hospital rather than prison after his sentencing for murder, defence mental health experts testified on Tuesday.
Du Pont, 58, is expected to be sentenced later in the day for the January 1996 murder of Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.

In February he was found guilty but mentally ill of the murder, a verdict that made him subject to a criminal penalty but allowed him to receive treatment before serving the remainder of any sentence in prison.
He faced a maximum sentence of 40 years for the conviction.

At Tuesday's sentencing hearing in state Court of Common Pleas, defence psychologist Gerald Cooke said recent examinations revealed du Pont to be improving under medication but in danger of relapse. "Currently he suffers from schizophrenia, paranoid type, which is now in a partial but tenuous remission," Cooke said.
Du Pont was benefiting from both the medication and therapy at the Norristown state psychiatric facility where the chemicals fortune heir was being held, he said.

He said du Pont would probably need medication for the rest of his life, adding that a prison environment could endanger his recovery and make him a threat to himself or others if he was subjected to undue stress or his medication were allowed to lapse.

Prosecutors, however, sought to show du Pont had recovered to the point where he could begin serving his term in prison. A letter from the Norristown facility said du Pont was capable of being moved to a prison.
And prosecution psychiatrist Dr. John O'Brien said after examining du Pont, "I do not see that there is any active (set of symptoms) which would warrant further patient hospitalization."
Were du Pont a patient in an ordinary psychiatric hospital and not a convicted killer, he said, "he would have been discharged by now."
Du Pont sat through the hearing more neatly groomed than during the course of his trial earlier this year. His hair and beard, long and shaggy during the trial, were closely cropped.
He nodded slowly through much of the proceeding, his mouth opening and closing at a similar pace as his head moved.

Du Pont is a great-great grandson of E.I. du Pont, who in 1802 founded the chemical firm that bears his name and spawned one of America's largest family fortunes. John du Pont's personal wealth has been estimated at up to $250 million.
